Neonatal western harvest mice emerge from the birth canal weighing approximately 1.33 grams [Wwb = approximately 1.33 grams], a modest mass characteristic of altricial murid rodents. This initial wet weight at birth, representing the culmination of a gestation period lasting 23 days [tg = 23 days] when females are maintained at a core body temperature of 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C], places the species at the lower end of the typical range for its genus. The altricial condition of the newborn, with closed eyes and sparse pelage, necessitates an extended period of maternal investment following parturition.

The transition from milk dependency to nutritional independence in Reithrodontomys megalotis occurs through the weaning process, marking the cessation of nursing. Under controlled laboratory conditions at a standard thermoneutral temperature of 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C], the time since birth at weaning has been documented at 21 days [tx = 21 days]. This relatively rapid weaning age aligns with the species' overall fast-paced life history strategy, allowing females to quickly return to reproductive condition. The suckling juvenile's digestive system undergoes a fundamental dietary transition during this period, shifting from the efficient assimilation of maternal milk to the processing of seeds and arthropods that comprise the adult diet. The successful achievement of nutritional emancipation at 3 weeks of age is a critical milestone, as it marks the onset of the pre-reproductive juvenile phase.

Female western harvest mice attain a maximum adult body mass of 11 grams [Wwi = 11 grams], a value that reflects the species' position among the smaller-bodied members of the Cricetidae family. This ultimate wet weight for females is reached after a period of post-weaning growth, during which the immature individual accumulates somatic tissues before reproductive activation. The relatively low adult body mass, compared to larger-bodied congeners, is associated with a high surface-area-to-volume ratio that imposes substantial thermoregulatory demands. Consequently, the basal metabolic rate is elevated to meet these challenges; respirometry trials conducted at a body temperature of 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C] have measured a resting oxygen consumption of 20.65 milliliters per hour [JOi = 20.65 milliliters per hour]. This maximal BMR underscores the high energetic cost of maintaining homeothermy in such a diminutive mammal.

The reproductive output of Reithrodontomys megalotis is characterized by a combination of moderate litter size and high annual fecundity. Breeding females produce 3.3 pups per litter [N_R_i = 3.3 pups per litter] and are capable of raising up to 4.5 litters per year [F_R_i = up to 4.5 litters per year], a prodigious annual reproductive effort that compensates for the species' relatively short life expectancy. These values, recorded when females are held at a stable body temperature of 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C], translate into a high potential for population growth in favorable habitats. The ability to initiate successive breeding events rapidly following parturition is facilitated by a brief gestation period and a postpartum estrus, enabling females to maximize the number of offspring produced during a single breeding season.

Longevity records for the western harvest mouse indicate a maximum lifespan of 3.6 years [am = 3.6 years] under captive conditions when animals are maintained at a consistent body temperature of 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C]. This lifespan, equivalent to approximately 1,314 days, represents a relatively short duration for a rodent of its body size, consistent with the species' r-selected life history. Puberty is attained relatively early in life, with females reaching sexual maturity at 107 days after birth [tp = 107 days after birth] at a temperature of 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C]. This rapid maturation allows young born early in the breeding season to themselves reproduce before the onset of winter, contributing to the species' capacity for irruptive population dynamics in response to favorable environmental conditions.
